```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import patsy

# --- Log vs level illustration, reusing the workshop's used-cars data ---
# GitHub raw URL (once pushed to the student data repo):
# cars_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/used_cars_chicago.csv")
cars_df = pd.read_csv("data/used_cars_chicago.csv")

level_model = smf.ols("price ~ age + agesq", data=cars_df).fit()
log_model = smf.ols("lnprice ~ age + agesq", data=cars_df).fit()

_pred_car = pd.DataFrame({"age": [10], "agesq": [100]})
level_pred = float(level_model.predict(_pred_car).iloc[0])
log_pred_raw = float(np.exp(log_model.predict(_pred_car).iloc[0]))
sigma2 = float(np.var(log_model.resid, ddof=log_model.df_model + 1))
log_pred_corrected = log_pred_raw * np.exp(sigma2 / 2)

log_level_rows = [
    {"label": "Point prediction", "log_model": f"${log_pred_raw:,.0f}", "corrected": f"${log_pred_corrected:,.0f}", "level_model": f"${level_pred:,.0f}"},
]

# --- Airbnb Hackney case study ---
# Source: Bekes & Kezdi's public airbnb dataset, osf.io/qyca8, filtered to the Hackney
# borough workfile and matched to their published N=4,393 case study sample.
# GitHub raw URL (once pushed to the student data repo):
# air_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/airbnb_hackney.csv")
air_df = pd.read_csv("data/airbnb_hackney.csv")
air_df = air_df.loc[:, ~air_df.columns.duplicated()]
amenity_cols = [c for c in air_df.columns if c.startswith("d_")]
air_df["n_accommodates2"] = air_df["n_accommodates"] ** 2
air_df["n_days_since2"] = air_df["n_days_since"] ** 2

air_formulas = {
    "M1": "price ~ n_accommodates",
    "M2": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type)",
    "M3": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type)",
    "M4": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_accommodates2 + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type) + n_days_since + n_days_since2",
    "M5": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_accommodates2 + n_beds + C(f_room_type)*C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type) + n_days_since + n_days_since2",
}
air_formulas["M6"] = air_formulas["M5"] + " + " + " + ".join(amenity_cols)

air_fitted = {name: smf.ols(f, data=air_df).fit() for name, f in air_formulas.items()}

def _rmse(m):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(m.resid ** 2)))

air_kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=20260921)
air_cv = {name: [] for name in air_formulas}
for tr_idx, te_idx in air_kf.split(air_df):
    train, test = air_df.iloc[tr_idx], air_df.iloc[te_idx]
    for name, f in air_formulas.items():
        m = smf.ols(f, data=train).fit()
        pred = m.predict(test)
        air_cv[name].append(float(np.sqrt(np.mean((test["price"] - pred) ** 2))))
air_cv_avg = {name: float(np.mean(v)) for name, v in air_cv.items()}

air_stats_rows = [
    {"Model": name, "N coef": len(air_fitted[name].params), "R2": round(air_fitted[name].rsquared, 2),
     "Training RMSE": round(_rmse(air_fitted[name]), 1), "CV RMSE": round(air_cv_avg[name], 1),
     "BIC": int(round(air_fitted[name].bic))}
    for name in air_formulas
]

air_complexity_data = []
for name in air_formulas:
    ncoef = len(air_fitted[name].params)
    air_complexity_data.append({"n_coef": ncoef, "rmse": round(_rmse(air_fitted[name]), 1), "series": "Training RMSE", "model": name})
    air_complexity_data.append({"n_coef": ncoef, "rmse": round(air_cv_avg[name], 1), "series": "Cross-validated RMSE", "model": name})

# --- LASSO on the M6 feature set ---
y, X = patsy.dmatrices(air_formulas["M6"], data=air_df, return_type="dataframe")
y = y.values.ravel()
X = X.drop(columns=["Intercept"])
scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs = scaler.fit_transform(X)
lasso = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=20260921, max_iter=20000).fit(Xs, y)
lasso_pred = lasso.predict(Xs)
lasso_rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y - lasso_pred) ** 2)))
n_nonzero = int(np.sum(lasso.coef_ != 0))
n_total = len(lasso.coef_)

lasso_kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=20260921)
lasso_cv_rmses = []
for tr_idx, te_idx in lasso_kf.split(Xs):
    lm = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=20260921, max_iter=20000).fit(Xs[tr_idx], y[tr_idx])
    pred = lm.predict(Xs[te_idx])
    lasso_cv_rmses.append(float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y[te_idx] - pred) ** 2))))
lasso_cv_rmse = float(np.mean(lasso_cv_rmses))

top_coefs = (
    pd.Series(lasso.coef_, index=X.columns)
    .loc[lambda s: s != 0]
    .abs()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(8)
)
_coef_labels = {c: c.replace("C(f_room_type)", "Room type").replace("C(f_property_type)", "Property type")
                  .replace("[T.", ": ").replace("]", "").replace(":", " x ") for c in top_coefs.index}
lasso_top_rows = [{"variable": _coef_labels.get(name, name), "importance": round(val, 2)} for name, val in top_coefs.items()]

lasso_code_output = (
    ">>> lasso = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X_scaled, y)\n"
    f">>> lasso.alpha_\n{lasso.alpha_:.3f}\n\n"
    f">>> (lasso.coef_ != 0).sum()   # variables kept out of {n_total}\n{n_nonzero}\n\n"
    f">>> np.sqrt(np.mean((y - lasso.predict(X_scaled))**2))   # in-sample RMSE\n{lasso_rmse:.1f}"
)

# --- Holdout diagnostics: predicted vs actual on held-out data, best OLS model (M6) ---
_rng = np.random.RandomState(20260921)
_holdout_mask = _rng.rand(len(air_df)) < 0.2
work_df = air_df.loc[~_holdout_mask].copy()
holdout_df = air_df.loc[_holdout_mask].copy()
m6_work = smf.ols(air_formulas["M6"], data=work_df).fit()
holdout_pred = m6_work.predict(holdout_df)
holdout_rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((holdout_df["price"] - holdout_pred) ** 2)))

yyhat_data = [
    {"actual": float(a), "predicted": float(p)}
    for a, p in zip(holdout_df["price"], holdout_pred)
    if a < 300 and p < 300
]

ojs_define(
    log_level_rows      = log_level_rows,
    air_stats_rows       = air_stats_rows,
    air_complexity_data  = air_complexity_data,
    lasso_code_output    = lasso_code_output,
    lasso_top_rows       = lasso_top_rows,
    lasso_rmse           = round(lasso_rmse, 1),
    lasso_cv_rmse        = round(lasso_cv_rmse, 1),
    n_nonzero            = n_nonzero,
    n_total              = n_total,
    holdout_rmse         = round(holdout_rmse, 1),
    yyhat_data           = yyhat_data,
)
```

# Label engineering {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Choosing the target's functional form

---

## Log or level?

- When price is the target, its relationship with predictors is often closer to linear once expressed as $\ln(price)$
- Log differences approximate relative (percentage) differences — often more stable across a wide price range
- Technical bonus: log prices are often closer to normally distributed, which helps a linear regression approximate the average well

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## The correction that's easy to forget

If the target was modelled in logs, the model predicts $\widehat{\ln y}$ — not $\hat y$. Simply exponentiating **underestimates** the average:

$$\hat y_j = e^{\widehat{\ln y}_j} \times e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}$$

- $e^{\widehat{\ln y}}$ alone recovers the *median*, not the mean
- The correction term adjusts for the spread of the regression's residuals — bigger residual variance, bigger correction
- Skipping it silently biases every prediction downward

## On our own data

```{.python}
level_model = smf.ols("price ~ age + agesq", data=df).fit()
log_model = smf.ols("lnprice ~ age + agesq", data=df).fit()

log_pred_raw = np.exp(log_model.predict(car))          # median, not mean
corrected = log_pred_raw * np.exp(sigma2 / 2)           # corrected mean
```

```{ojs}
{
  return html`<table style="margin:20px auto 0;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1.1em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;"><th style="padding:6px 22px;"></th><th style="padding:6px 22px;">Log model, uncorrected</th><th style="padding:6px 22px;">Log model, corrected</th><th style="padding:6px 22px;">Level model</th></tr>
    ${log_level_rows.map(d => `<tr><td style="padding:5px 22px;">${d.label}</td><td style="padding:5px 22px;text-align:center;">${d.log_model}</td><td style="padding:5px 22px;text-align:center;font-weight:700;">${d.corrected}</td><td style="padding:5px 22px;text-align:center;">${d.level_model}</td></tr>`).join('')}
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
For a 10-year-old Camry, the raw log prediction and the level-model prediction disagree — the correction closes most of that gap.
:::

# Feature engineering {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Building the right-hand side

---

## The checklist

1. **Missing values** — random, or systematic? Impute with a flag column, don't just drop the observation
2. **Categorical values** — binary, or a small set of dummies
3. **Text** — mine it for useful signal (a "seminar" keyword, say), otherwise leave it
4. **Functional form** — polynomials, splines, logs — the same choices as the workshop, applied to many variables at once
5. **Interactions** — worth thinking about, expensive to search exhaustively

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## Real data: Airbnb, London

- 4,393 Hackney-borough listings, March 2017 snapshot
- Target: nightly `price` (USD)
- ~70 predictor candidates: capacity, room and property type, cancellation policy, review scores, and 50 individual amenity dummies (`d_tv`, `d_petsallowed`, `d_elevatorinbuilding`, ...)

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), airbnb dataset, osf.io/qyca8
:::

## Six models, built up by hand

```{.python}
M1 = smf.ols("price ~ n_accommodates", data=df).fit()
M2 = smf.ols("price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type)", data=df).fit()
M3 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type)", data=df).fit()
M4 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + n_accommodates2 + n_days_since + n_days_since2", data=df).fit()
M5 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + C(f_room_type)*C(f_property_type)", data=df).fit()
M6 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + " + " + ".join(amenity_dummies), data=df).fit()  # 50 amenities
```

Each step adds more: capacity and type, then physical features, then non-linearity and interactions, then every amenity.

# Selecting variables automatically {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## LASSO

---

## We can't try every model

- With $p$ candidate predictors, the number of possible models explodes — this is an **NP-hard** problem, not just a big one
- **By hand**: domain knowledge drives the choice — interpretable, but slow, and impossible with many interactions
- **By algorithm**: let the data suggest which variables earn their place

## The LASSO idea

LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) adds a penalty to the usual OLS minimisation:

$$\min_\beta \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_j x_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{k}|\beta_j| \right\}$$

- The penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero
- Coefficients whose inclusion barely improves fit get shrunk **all the way** to zero — dropped from the model entirely
- $\lambda$ controls how aggressive that is; larger $\lambda$, fewer surviving variables

## The cost: bias

- OLS is unbiased. LASSO isn't — that's the trade it makes for lower variance
- Unlike OLS, there's no closed-form solution; an algorithm solves for $\beta$ and $\lambda$ together
- $\lambda$ itself is chosen by cross-validation: try many values, pick the one with the best CV RMSE

::: {.fragment}
Ridge regression is the same idea with a squared penalty ($\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$) instead — it shrinks coefficients but never sets them exactly to zero. LASSO is "L1," Ridge is "L2."
:::

## LASSO on the Airbnb data

```{.python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)   # LASSO needs standardised features
lasso = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X_scaled, y)
```

```{ojs}
html`<pre style="font-family:'SF Mono','Menlo',monospace;font-size:0.68em;line-height:1.4;
                  background:#f6f6f8;border:1px solid #e0e0e6;border-radius:6px;
                  padding:8px 14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;">${lasso_code_output}</pre>`
```

```{ojs}
html`<div class="instructions-box">LASSO kept ${n_nonzero} of ${n_total} candidate coefficients — automatically — and its cross-validated RMSE (${lasso_cv_rmse}) lands close to M6's OLS fit, with far fewer moving parts.</div>`
```

# Post-prediction diagnostics {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Holdout sets

---

## One more split before you trust the number

- Model selection (BIC, cross-validation) already uses the data — repeatedly
- Best practice: carve off a **holdout set** right at the start, and don't touch it until the very end
- **Work set**: model building, model selection, training/test folds — all happen here
- **Holdout set**: touched exactly once, to get an honest read on how the chosen model will do on genuinely new data

## The workflow

1. Split the original data into a work set and a holdout set
2. Inside the work set: training/test folds, k-fold CV, model selection
3. Re-estimate the winning model on the *whole* work set
4. Apply it to the holdout set — untouched until now
5. Evaluate: this is the honest estimate of live-data performance

## Predicted vs. actual, on the holdout set

:::: {.shrink-on-reveal data-frag="wk10online-yyhat-frag" style="--large-height:600px;--small-height:420px;--shrink-scale:0.7;"}
::: {.shrink-on-reveal-inner}
```{ojs}

  width: 620, height: 600,
  x: {label: "Predicted price ($)", domain: [0, 300]},
  y: {label: "Actual price ($)", domain: [0, 300]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{x:0,y:0},{x:300,y:300}], {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.dot(yyhat_data, {x: "predicted", y: "actual", fill: "#2c3e7a", opacity: 0.4, r: 3})
  ]
})
```
:::
::::

```{ojs}
html`<div class="fragment" id="wk10online-yyhat-frag">Holdout RMSE: <b>$${holdout_rmse}</b>. Points above the dashed line are underpredicted; the model visibly struggles more at the high end — the same pattern Gabor & Kézdi find in their own version of this diagnostic.</div>`
```

## Summary

- Prediction with many candidate variables needs the same discipline as prediction with a few — just automated where hand-picking becomes infeasible
- Log targets need a correction term before converting back — skipping it silently biases predictions down
- LASSO trades a little bias for a lot less variance, and does variable selection as a side effect
- A holdout set, touched only once, is the honest final check — everything before it is negotiable, this isn't
